Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic forecast errors and derive correction rules.

Looking at the data, I can see this is about EU ETS (carbon market) price forecasting with a 30-day horizon.

Let me examine the patterns:

**Example 1 (Dec 10, 2024)** - Most errors are that the model forecasts are TOO LOW compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the first few days:
- Model: [68.04, 68.31, 65.51, 63.63, 64.16, 62.98, 63.49, 66.10, 66.34, 67.38, 66.79, 68.28, 68.34, 69.00, 70.80, 71.01, 69.10, 68.31, 65.91, 66.30, 66.90, 67.94, 67.40, 67.49, 67.08, 67.11, 66.96, 66.49, 64.74, 65.21
- True: [68.18, 68.63, 66.10, 64.43, 65.27, 64.26, 64.86, 67.69, 68.20, 69.68, 69.47, 71.56, 71.98, 73.00, 75.19, 75.94, 74.36, 74.04, 72.17, 73.46, 74.85, 76.92, 76.96, 77.98, 78.33, 79.26, 79.99, 80.27, 78.94, 80.76

The model is consistently below true prices, especially after day 12 where the divergence grows significantly. The true prices seem to be trending up more strongly than the model predicts.


I notice a clear sentiment-driven pattern emerging. When market sentiment shifts from negative to positive, the model underestimates price momentum. Specifically, positive sentiment spikes aren't being fully captured - the model lags behind real price movements, particularly during periods of increasing enthusiasm. The divergence becomes more pronounced as prices climb, suggesting the model may be too conservative in anticipating market dynamics.
